clue.text: Cheer a drop goal that's going over line

indicators.note: the goal piece goes over, i.e. past, the line piece, so it is placed after it

parts.note: CC, a cubic centimetre, is a drop of liquid in measuring terms
an aim is a goal or target

explanation.surface: Rugby fans roar as a drop goal sails over the line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drop goal' reads as one rugby term, but the two words do separate jobs; 'going over' means the goal piece passes beyond the line piece and so follows it.
explanation.definitionFit: To acclaim someone is to applaud or hail them, so it is a synonym of the verb cheer.

clue.text: A bird crossing lake — one first crossed pond

indicators.note: crossing means the bird is laid across the lake letter, which ends up inside it

parts.note: a cock is a male bird
L is the abbreviation for lake on maps

explanation.surface: A bird flies over a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: John Alcock, with Arthur Brown, made the first non-stop transatlantic flight in 1919; 'pond' is jokey slang for the Atlantic.
explanation.definitionFit: The aviator who piloted the first non-stop flight across the Atlantic, nicknamed the pond.

clue.text: Territories in Canada getting a good deal

parts.note: tons means a lot, a good deal

explanation.surface: Provinces in Canada are getting a favourable bargain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A good deal' reads as a bargain but means a large quantity.
explanation.definitionFit: These are administrative regions, as in Switzerland, so a synonym of territories or districts.

clue.text: Anti-royalist battle?

parts.note: the battle's name splits into a dialect word meaning against and the royal household, so it sounds like a fight opposing royalty

explanation.definitionFit: The 1415 battle in which Henry V defeated the French, whose name splits into dialect 'against' plus royal household.

clue.text: Half-length coat, one with dark turn-up

indicators.note: in a down clue, turn-up means the letters are read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one
dim means dark or poorly lit

explanation.surface: A mid-calf coat with a dark cuff turned up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn-up' suggests a trouser cuff, which suits the clothing surface, but it reverses I and DIM in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A midi is a garment reaching mid-calf, between a mini and a maxi in length.

clue.text: Mug duped, often heartlessly

parts.note: set up means framed or duped

indicators.note: heartlessly tells us to remove the middle of the word often, keeping only its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A gullible victim gets swindled again and again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mug' looks like a noun for a dupe, which fits the surface, but it is the verb: to mug is to attack.
explanation.definitionFit: To mug someone is to attack and rob them, the same as assault, a common phrasal-verb synonym.

clue.text: Melody maker: top periodical

parts.note: swell is dated slang for excellent, first-rate, top
an organ is a newspaper or magazine serving a group

explanation.surface: Melody Maker was a leading music magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: Melody Maker was a long-running British music weekly, which 'periodical' plays on; the answer is a division of a pipe organ.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a keyboard division of a pipe organ with shuttered pipes, an instrument that produces tunes.

clue.text: Hooker has little time by herself? Not altogether

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for time

indicators.note: not altogether means not the whole word, so its last letter is dropped

parts.note: by herself means alone

explanation.surface: A prostitute has a short time by herself, but not entirely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hooker' suggests a prostitute, but it means something that hooks: a bird of prey's claw.
explanation.definitionFit: A bird of prey's claw is curved for hooking its prey.

clue.text: Father has nothing in position for baby

parts.note: pa is an informal word for father

indicators.note: in means the letter for nothing goes inside the word for position

parts.note: a pose is a posture or position
O is zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A father adopts a pose holding his baby.
explanation.definitionFit: A word of Algonquian origin for a North American Indian baby or young child.

clue.text: One tuned in to family favourites

definitions.text: One tuned in to family favourites

parts.words: One tuned in to family favourites
parts.note: suggests a listener to a radio request show but means someone who favours relatives, giving them jobs

explanation.walkthrough: Family Favourites was a long-running BBC radio request programme, which the clue evokes.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone guilty of favouritism toward relatives, especially in appointments, is attuned to favouring kin.

clue.text: Speaker's forthright with prime minister: topping!

indicators.note: the speaker says the words, so we want what they sound like rather than how they are spelt

parts.note: forthright is candid, and Sir Robert Peel was a 19th-century British prime minister

explanation.surface: A Speaker of the Commons praises an outspoken prime minister.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark makes 'topping' look like old slang for splendid; it is literally a cake topping. 'Speaker's' also hints at the Commons Speaker.
explanation.definitionFit: Sugared citrus rind is used as a decoration sprinkled on cakes and puddings, so it is a topping.

clue.text: Spot one signals lieutenant

definitions.meaning: a small dot or mark, as on dice or playing cards
British army ranks are shown by small stars on the shoulder; a lieutenant wears two of them

explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are a small star or dot: a mark on a die, and an insignia star showing an officer's rank.

clue.text: Top quality snack from freezer, with cold centre scooped out

indicators.note: the middle letter is taken out of the frozen snack, as if scooped from its centre

parts.note: a choc ice is a chocolate-coated ice-cream bar, a British frozen treat
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps

explanation.surface: Delicious frozen treat, with the chilly middle eaten away.
explanation.walkthrough: A CHOC ICE is a British ice-cream bar coated in chocolate; its seven letters have C, the cold abbreviation, exactly at the centre.
explanation.definitionFit: Choice as an adjective means of the finest grade, select, as in choice cuts of meat.

clue.text: Intend to put pressure aside and get into bed

parts.note: to plan to do something is to intend to do it

indicators.note: the letter for pressure is set aside, removed from the word put

parts.note: taken as the word put
P is the physics symbol for pressure

explanation.surface: Someone decides not to rush things before getting into bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bed' is a flower bed, not sleep: young plants are set into the bed from pots.
explanation.definitionFit: Gardeners transfer seedlings from pots into flower beds, so setting them in the soil is what this phrasal verb means.

clue.text: Lotion man applied to terrible strain

indicators.note: terrible means the letters of strain are badly knocked about

parts.note: a gent is a gentleman, a man

explanation.surface: A man rubs lotion on to a terrible muscle strain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'terrible' is the anagram signal and 'applied to' simply attaches the man to the end; the surface's muscle strain is a red herring for the lotion.
explanation.definitionFit: An astringent is a skin tonic that tightens pores, applied as a liquid preparation.

clue.text: Court action put an end to fraudulent schemes

parts.note: to squash something is to suppress or quash it
rackets are dishonest money-making schemes

explanation.surface: A police operation shuts down a ring of swindles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Court action' suggests a lawsuit, but the court is a sports court with four walls.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the formal name of a racquet sport played on an enclosed court, so it is literally action on a court.

clue.text: When a car goes wrong, I'll be called in to provide service

indicators.note: be called in means the letter I is summoned inside the jumbled letters
goes wrong signals the letters of the preceding words are put into disorder

parts.note: the speaker's I, as in 'I will'

explanation.surface: A mechanic promises to be called out to service a broken-down car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'goes wrong' rearranges WHENACAR and 'be called in' puts I inside. 'Service' looks like car servicing but is a dinner service.
explanation.definitionFit: A set of matching porcelain plates and dishes is called a dinner service.

clue.text: Occurrence that is taking place about onset of dusk

definitions.text: Occurrence that is taking place about onset of dusk

parts.note: an event is an occurrence

indicators.note: about means placed around, so IE goes round the letter

parts.note: IE (id est) is the abbreviation for that is

indicators.note: the onset of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Something happening around the time darkness falls.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue defines the answer: an event at nightfall describes the time itself.
explanation.definitionFit: This poetic word means evening, the period when darkness begins to fall.

clue.text: Serving meat a blunder, entertaining one given to this?

definitions.text: Serving meat a blunder, entertaining one given to this?

indicators.note: entertaining means holding a guest, so the letter for one is held inside the jumble
blunder works as a verb here, sending the letters of the preceding words into a muddle

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A host serving meat to a guest who avoids it would be committing a blunder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blunder' rearranges SERVINGMEATA and 'entertaining' takes I inside. Read whole, the clue also defines the answer: someone given to this belief would find being served meat a gaffe.
explanation.definitionFit: The principle of not eating meat is the belief whose followers would see a meat dish as a social mistake.

clue.text: Put up massive stakes as gallows

indicators.note: put up in a down clue means the word for massive is written from the bottom upwards

parts.note: big means massive
bets are stakes wagered

explanation.surface: A gambler puts up huge stakes, with the gallows awaiting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stakes' suggests wooden posts like gallows, but it means wagers.
explanation.definitionFit: A gibbet is an upright post with an arm for hanging criminals, the same thing as gallows.

clue.text: Uneasy feeling of man crossing a small island

indicators.note: crossing means the word for man spans the other letters, holding them within

parts.note: male means a man
IS is the abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: A man feels uneasy as he crosses to a little island.
explanation.definitionFit: Malaise is a general sense of discomfort or unease.

clue.text: Physician's beginning treatment shortly with this?

definitions.text: Physician's beginning treatment shortly with this?

indicators.note: beginning means just the first letter of the doctor's word
shortly means cut short, so the last letter is lost

parts.note: a remedy is a treatment

explanation.surface: A doctor's about to start treating a patient after giving this.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue defines the answer: a sedative given before an operation, with which treatment shortly begins.
explanation.definitionFit: Short for premedication, a sedative drug given to a patient before surgery or anaesthesia.

clue.text: Stealing rich person's jewellery

parts.note: a nob is British slang for a wealthy or upper-class person
bling is flashy jewellery

explanation.surface: A thief takes a wealthy person's jewels.
explanation.walkthrough: NOB is British slang for a toff; the verb also means tampering with a racehorse, but here it is the British slang sense of pinching.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang this verb means to pinch or steal something, as well as to drug a racehorse.

clue.text: Don't touch — you need permission

definitions.meaning: to let something alone, not interfere with it
authorisation to be absent, as in time off granted

explanation.definitionFit: One word means to let alone, as in 'let it be', and also means granted permission, as in shore time off for a sailor.

clue.text: Old-fashioned screw needs brief jolt and trouble's contained

indicators.note: contained means one piece is held inside the other
brief means cut short, so the last letter comes off the word for jolt

parts.note: a jerk is a sudden jolt
to ail is to trouble; the 's stands for 'is'

explanation.surface: A warder of the old school gives a quick shake to keep trouble in check.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Screw' is British prison slang for a warder; 'Old-fashioned' marks the dated title for a prison keeper.
explanation.definitionFit: A screw in prison slang is a warder, and this is the older word for the person in charge of a prison.

clue.text: Youngster talked of pirate captain

indicators.note: talked of means spoken, so we want a word that sounds the same

parts.note: a kid is a youngster

explanation.surface: Children speak of a pirate captain in stories.
explanation.walkthrough: William Kidd was a notorious 17th-century Scottish pirate, Captain Kidd.
explanation.definitionFit: William Kidd was a privateer turned notorious buccaneer, hanged in 1701.

clue.text: Queen Elizabeth the first rejected passionate feeling

indicators.note: rejected means sent back, so the letters are read in the opposite direction

parts.note: Elizabeth I's royal cipher is ER (Elizabeth Regina) followed by the numeral I

explanation.surface: Elizabeth I spurned someone's ardent advances.
explanation.walkthrough: ER, for Elizabeth Regina, is the standard abbreviation for the Queen; 'the first' adds the numeral I.
explanation.definitionFit: Ire is anger, a strong and heated emotion.

clue.text: Uncle Sam's expression distorted by mini-cameras

indicators.note: distorted means twisted out of shape, so the letters of the cameras are rearranged

explanation.surface: Uncle Sam's face looks warped in photos taken by tiny cameras.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Expression' suggests a look on Uncle Sam's face, but it means a word or phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Uncle Sam personifies the United States, so a word or phrase typical of US usage is his expression.

clue.text: You'll need quantity of mince, as I estimate most like pie

indicators.note: a quantity of the words means only part of them is needed, a run of letters within

explanation.surface: A cook advises on how much mince to use in a pie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pie' suggests the mince filling, but it is the idiom 'easy as pie'.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'easy as pie' means very simple, so the superlative of easy is most pie-like.

clue.text: What's done with bird landing in part of pool?

indicators.note: landing in means the bird comes down inside the other word

parts.note: a deed is an act, something done
a pen is a female swan

explanation.surface: A bird splashes down into the swimming pool.
explanation.walkthrough: PEN, a female swan, is a crossword favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: The section of a swimming pool where the water is deepest is called by this name.
